newCard.subject: History
newCard.name: Leadership in early First Nation and Inuit communities
newCard.description: Know a bounded, source-attributed repertoire of early community organisation: the Haudenosaunee founding-peace account and council/Clan Mother relationships, and a qualified reconstruction of leadership, crews and resource sharing in a Classic Thule Inuit whaling community. Explain the different roles and cooperation relationships without turning a traditional account or archaeological model into a universal political system.
evidence: After study, identify the Haudenosaunee founding-peace account and explain the relationship between distinct Nations, chiefs, Clan Mothers and shared council decisions. Attribute the account and distinguish its historical peace aim from a modern municipal council or one all-powerful ruler.

Describe the studied Classic Thule community reconstruction: organising cooperative harvesting involved leaders, crews and household/resource relationships. Explain the supported link between coordination, resource access and social roles/status, labelling the archaeological/analogy-based interpretation rather than claiming an observed constitution for every Inuit community.

Compare the two learned arrangements with a supported similarity and difference. Given a fresh attributed community account, use its own role/decision information instead of assuming the first case’s institutions or a fixed system based on ethnicity or region.
newCard.assessmentPrompt: After learning the Haudenosaunee founding account and the studied early Inuit community reconstruction, can {{name}} explain who worked together, how roles differed and what cooperation helped achieve? Compare the cases, then offer a new attributed account: what can they conclude, and what remains uncertain?

pedagogy.summary: Teach two particular historical organisation arrangements with source roles and uncertainty attached; do not replace knowledge with generic good-leadership advice.
bestPractices: Separate named community relationships before comparing them.
Make the basis of a traditional account and a research reconstruction visible.
Require explanation of who cooperates/decides and why, not a list of political labels.
keyRepresentations: A broad place/time strip with an uncertain founding date clearly marked
A new supplied community account for bounded comparison
commonMisconceptions: Every Indigenous community was governed in the same way.
A council must be an elected municipality or a chief must be an absolute pharaoh.
An archaeological model is an eyewitness law code and proves everybody’s gender/status.
Cooperation means no disagreement occurred or every peace attempt succeeded.

learn.summary: Learn the two case-specific organisation relationships, then retrieve and compare them with explicit source limits.

activities.title: Explain two early community organisation arrangements
learnerActions: Prepare two separate attributed case records. For the Haudenosaunee case, distinguish the Nations’ founding-peace account from continuing traditional institutions and present policies. For Qariaraqyuk, separate dated archaeological occupation/evidence from the researcher’s model using later analogies. Use original age-appropriate summaries and lawful source links, not copied source stories or invented historical dialogue.

Teach the Haudenosaunee account as an alliance of distinct Nations seeking peaceful shared decision-making. Use Onondaga and another named founding Nation as concrete examples without requiring a complete membership or chief-name inventory. Connect chiefs and Clan Mothers with community well-being, and distinguish nation affairs from shared council concerns in the continuing traditional description. No precise founding year is required or independently established.

Teach the bounded Classic Thule interpretation: a leader/boat organiser and cooperating crew coordinated harvesting and shares/resources, with differing household access/status. Show why a large communal task needs coordination and distinguish that explanatory relationship from a claim about every person’s wealth, gender or authority. The published research uses North Alaskan analogy and material differences; it is not an eyewitness Qariaraqyuk law code.

Build two simple relationship diagrams using named roles, arrows for the supported decision/cooperation/resource relationship and a clear source label. A diagram of one case must not simply be copied onto the other. Existing generic role and comparison skills support this knowledge but do not supply the particular historical facts.

After supported study, remove the completed diagrams/captions and ask the learner to explain each arrangement in ordinary language, with drawing/pointing support where useful. Check actual role relationships and purposes, not pronunciation of every unfamiliar title or memorisation of an exact date.

Compare what cooperation aimed to achieve in the two cases: attributed founding peace/shared decisions and modelled coordinated harvesting/resource relations. Do not turn cooperation into proof that conflict never occurred or that a documented response always succeeded. An actual Inuit conflict-resolution attempt remains a separate source condition for A3.10.

Provide a new attributed account with its own roles and decisions. Ask for a supported comparison and a question still unanswered. Repeat with a changed representation of a learned case to distinguish particular knowledge from copying or an assumption that all Indigenous communities share one system.
activities.intendedInsight: Historical communities organised authority, cooperation and resources through particular relationships; shared needs do not make their institutions identical.
feedback: Ask which named case and source supports the role relationship.
Return to the separate diagrams if the learner moves a council, title or authority rule from one case to the other.
Retain uncertainty where an inference or chronology is not directly documented.
activities.rationale: Original untested teaching design; factual-source verification is distinct from intervention efficacy.
sourceClaims: The Nation’s attributed founding account links formerly warring Nations, a Grand Council of chiefs and Clan Mothers with working together for peace and community well-being. Its proposed founding date is an estimate.
The Confederacy presents its own founding account and traditional nation-council/Grand-Council relationship, identifies Clan Mothers’ role, and states that the exact founding date is unknown.

Research at Qariaraqyuk supports a bounded early Inuit community case with substantial 14th-century occupation. Leadership, crew, resource-sharing and household-status relations are interpreted through archaeology and explicit later North Alaskan analogies, not directly recorded as an early constitution.

constraints: The required learned repertoire remains the attributed Haudenosaunee founding/council relationship and the bounded Classic Thule community reconstruction. Additional supplied source-reviewed cases may support comparison and transfer; they do not replace either required arrangement or change this stable claim’s knowledge.

The exact Haudenosaunee foundation date is unknown in the Confederacy account; Onondaga’s approximate estimate is attributed, not asserted as an independently established year. Do not backdate every current department, legal policy or chief-selection detail to a precise pre-1500 village.

No Droulers-government inference, universal Inuit constitution, fixed gender rule, compulsory cultural participation or ceremony/whaling reenactment. No complete legal text, five-Nation roster or present constitutional-rights adjudication is required.

The material-life claim stays unchanged. Governance/social/cooperation contributions do not by themselves complete all early-societies comparisons, young-person duties or the A3.10 conflict-resolution conjunction.
Source-specific historical interpretation is not a new general research-method claim or automatic learner mastery. Teaching efficacy is untested.

assess.correctAnswer: Identifies both learned arrangements and explains the different supported role/cooperation relationships, source basis and limits; compares a supplied new account without making one system universal.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Removing the completed diagram checks particular historical knowledge rather than copying or generic cooperation advice. Contrasting shared goals with different role arrangements exposes an assumed universal council/hierarchy, while a new attributed account and model label test bounded transfer rather than certainty from ethnicity.
probeDeeper: Which community and account does that role belong to?
What did that cooperation aim to achieve, and what does the source actually support?
Is this a traditional historical account, a modern institution description or an archaeological reconstruction?

errorPatterns.pattern: One generic government type replaces both actual arrangements.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the Grand Council a modern municipal service council or assigns a pharaoh to the whaling community.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the two named diagrams and explain one supported difference.

errorPatterns.pattern: Turns an analogy or uncertain chronology into a precisely observed universal fact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims all Inuit households followed a documented constitution or assigns every current policy to an exact founding year.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate observed evidence, the source’s account and modelled interpretation; keep only the supported relationship.

responseLevels.gap: Only generic leadership/council labels or universal stereotypes.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls some roles but confuses case relationships, purposes or source certainty.
responseLevels.full: Explains both particular arrangements and their supported cooperation relationships, retains attribution/uncertainty, and compares a supplied account without importing institutions.
